name: Aegyo-sal (eye smile) filler or surgery

lead: Aegyo-sal, also called pretarsal fullness or the charming roll, is a soft roll just above the lower lash line that is considered aesthetically desirable in East Asian culture because it makes the lower lid look youthful and expressive. Some people have it naturally and others build it.

It can be created with filler placed in the correct tissue planes, or with surgery. A 2025 review describes anatomy-based filler techniques for it, and a surgical series reported measurable increases in pretarsal protrusion.

paras: Practitioners in clinics inject filler to build the roll, or perform surgical approaches such as plication of the capsulopalpebral fascia with an implant. The review emphasises precise placement in the right tissue plane for a natural-looking result tailored to individual anatomy.

Periorbital filler and surgery carry complication risks, which the 2025 review says anatomical technique is meant to avoid. Results are individual, and a 2026 surgical outcomes paper on the topic is listed as retracted.

web.title: Aegyo Sal: the K-beauty Trend for Bigger Looking Eyes

chain: Filler or implant builds a small roll under the lower lashes
Lower lid looks fuller and more youthful
angle.text: The roll beneath the lash line is used to make the eyes look youthful and friendly, and its absence is described as contributing to a tired or aged appearance.[3] Clinics place filler or perform surgery to add it, and makeup can imitate it temporarily.

lead: Aegyo-sal, also known as pretarsal fullness or the "charming roll," is a soft roll above the lower lash line that enhances a youthful and expressive look of the lower eyelid and is considered desirable in East Asian culture.[1] The term comes from Korean: aegyo (애교) is the word for a cute, affectionate manner of expression, and the feature is known in English as the "eye smile."[2] The roll becomes more visible when a person smiles, which is why it is associated with a friendly, smiling look.[3]

People who do not have the roll naturally can build it. Clinics describe injecting small amounts of hyaluronic acid filler just beneath the lower lash line, using makeup or tapes as temporary alternatives, and, in surgical practice, fat grafting or implants.[3][1][4] A 2025 review by Korean plastic surgeons describes anatomy-based filler injection for both supraorbital hollowness (the sunken upper eyelid) and the charming roll, stressing placement within the correct tissue planes to avoid complications and achieve natural results.[1] People who have a prominent natural roll but would like less of it are also catered to: one clinic notes that low-dose botulinum toxin can relax the muscle underneath.[3]

The trend sits inside a broader history of eyelid aesthetics in East Asia: since Mikamo developed double eyelid surgery in the late 19th century, the ideal periorbital appearance has evolved, and South Korea is the country that most often changes the eye in all four directions: upper, lower, medial and lateral.[5] South Korea has the highest per-capita rate of elective cosmetic surgery in the world according to ISAPS figures cited by Wikipedia, and the aegyo-sal look is part of a wider set of eye-area procedures offered there.[6]

paras: Pretarsal fullness is a roll above the lash line of the lower lid. The 2025 review calls it a significant feature of periorbital aesthetics that conveys youth and expressiveness.[1] It is not the same as the lower-eyelid bag or the tear trough hollow beneath it; the sunken or tired look of the lower lid region is generally associated with fat prolapse, volume loss and the eyelid-cheek junction, while aegyo-sal sits closer to the lashes.[7]

One Singapore clinic's patient guide states that the roll is not skin but a part of the orbicularis oculi, the ring-shaped muscle around the eye, and that eye bags arise from pseudoherniation of orbital fat, whereas aegyo-sal reflects muscle bulk.[3] The orbicularis oculi has a pretarsal portion lying over the tarsal plate of the lid, which is thought to drive spontaneous blinking, and its contraction on smiling is what makes the roll appear more prominent.[8]

The Korean word aegyo more broadly refers to a performance of cute affection in speech, voice and facial expression, which is expected of K-pop idols and younger women in Korean society and has been linked by scholars to gendered expectations; the eye-smile feature takes its name from that cultural register.[2]

Asian eyelid aesthetics have been reshaped since the late 19th century, when Mikamo developed the double eyelid technique, and the 2015 Seminars in Plastic Surgery review describes four vectors of change: upper, lower, medial and lateral. South Korea is described there as the only country that most often uses all four.[5] The lower vector, which includes the pretarsal roll and tear trough, is therefore part of a standard repertoire of eye procedures there.

Wikipedia's account of cosmetic surgery in South Korea traces interest in appearance to the physiognomy belief of gwansang, notes that American doctors introduced plastic-surgery techniques during the Korean War, and links growth in procedures to labour-market competition after the 1997 financial crisis and to the global spread of K-pop and K-drama.[6] In 2018 an estimated 464,452 medical tourists visited South Korea for cosmetic surgery, according to the same article.[6] Double eyelid surgery and rhinoplasty are listed as leading procedures; fillers are not discussed in detail there.[6]
A Singapore clinic describes the roll as a K-beauty look and lists makeup, face tapes and stickers among the ways people imitate it.[3]

Filler. The 2025 review treats the plane of placement as critical to a natural result and to avoiding complications, and it pairs treatment of the roll with correction of supraorbital hollowness because both are common reasons for an aged or tired upper-face impression in East Asians.[1] Clinics describe small volumes of hyaluronic acid filler placed just below the lower lash line as an office procedure with limited downtime, with swelling and bruising as the effects most often mentioned.[3] Filler is distinct from neurotoxins; in the US it is regulated as a medical device that must be administered by a licensed provider, whereas in the UK and EEA it is a CE-marked device that a licensed person may inject.[9]

Surgery. Surgical routes include capsulopalpebral fascia plication combined with a silicone prosthesis implant, described in a retrospective series of 68 patients (91.2% female, mean age 32.6) at one institution between August 2021 and August 2024, in which pretarsal protrusion increased from 1.2 to 2.9 mm and no major complications or conversions were reported. That paper is marked as retracted on PubMed.[4] Fat grafts and implants are listed by one clinic as further surgical options.[3]

Related eye-area techniques include two-dimensional micro-fat injection for tear trough deformity in younger patients and fat grafting for dark-circle exacerbation after lower blepharoplasty, which target neighbouring areas rather than the roll itself.[10][11] Lower blepharoplasty generally can be performed through a skin or conjunctival incision and may be combined with canthopexy and fat repositioning at the eyelid-cheek junction.[7]
Non-procedural options. Makeup, face tapes and stickers can imitate the roll temporarily. A clinic page cautions that tapes may abrade the skin.[3]

Periorbital filler carries the general risks of dermal filler injection: bruising, redness, swelling and pain are common; infection, allergic reactions and lumps are less common; and accidental injection into a vessel can cause skin necrosis or, rarely, blindness through retrograde embolisation, which Wikipedia describes as usually permanent.[9] The 2025 review's emphasis on anatomy-based placement is framed as a way to reduce such complications.[1]

Surgery in this region has its own risks. The 2026 fat-grafting paper notes that lower eyelid blepharoplasty, a widely performed procedure, is associated with complications such as lower eyelid retraction and malposition, and that dark circles can be exacerbated afterwards.[11] In Korea more broadly, 'ghost surgery', in which an unlicensed substitute operates while the patient is anaesthetised, has been a regulatory concern, and the operating-room camera law of 2021 was a response.[6]

The 2025 review covers filler technique for this area and is a descriptive, technique-focused paper rather than a controlled trial.[1] A retrospective surgical series of 68 patients reported improved protrusion, curvature and aperture, with a mean operative time of 46.3 minutes, but the publication is retracted.[4]

Studies of neighbouring techniques include a series of 102 young patients (mean age 25.9) who received two-dimensional micro-fat injection for tear trough deformity, with significant improvement maintained during follow-up, and a series of 32 patients who underwent autologous fat grafting after lower blepharoplasty, with patient-reported improvement in dark circles on a 5-point scale.[10][11] No randomised trial of aegyo-sal filler versus control or study of perceived age or attractiveness after the procedure has been published.

Aegyo-sal is discussed mainly through K-beauty media and clinic marketing rather than a single forum community. A Singapore aesthetic clinic markets filler for the feature as a youthful K-beauty look, and notes that people who prefer a smaller natural roll can ask for muscle relaxation instead.[3] In Korea the look sits within a wider culture of eye-area cosmetic procedures, with beauty standards criticised by some commentators as unrealistic and linked to pressure on women, as Wikipedia reports.[6]

lore.intro: Claims about aegyo-sal come mainly from clinic pages, K-beauty content and the plastic surgery literature rather than a single forum movement.[3][1]

claims.claim: The roll makes the eyes look youthful and friendly
Aegyo-sal is a muscle feature, not an eye bag
Where filler is placed determines whether the result looks natural
Surgery with an implant can durably increase the roll
Makeup or tape can imitate the look without a procedure
The roll can be relaxed with neuromodulator if it is unwanted

timeline.event: Karl Ferdinand von Gräfe coins the term blepharoplasty for eyelid surgery.[7]
Mikamo develops the double eyelid (blepharoplasty) technique for Asian eyes.[5]
American doctors introduce plastic-surgery techniques in South Korea during the Korean War.[6]
The Asian financial crisis and labour-market changes are linked to a rise in cosmetic surgery for competitive advantage.[6]
Seminars in Plastic Surgery review describes four vectors of change in Asian eyelid aesthetics, with South Korea using all four.[5]
464,452 medical tourists visit South Korea for cosmetic surgery, a 16.7% rise on 2017.[6]
South Korea has the highest per-capita rate of elective cosmetic surgery by ISAPS data; operating-room cameras are mandated after ghost-surgery scandals.[6]
Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology publishes a series of 102 young patients treated for tear trough deformity with fat injections.[10]
Life (Basel) review describes anatomy-based filler injection for supraorbital hollowness and the charming roll.[1]
A Medicine paper on pretarsal fullness surgery in 68 patients is retracted.[4]
